newsitem.title: UK: East Timor's Horta welcomes new British attitude.
newsitem.headline: East Timor's Horta welcomes new British attitude.

text.p: East Timorese independence leader and Nobel peace prize winner Jose Ramos Horta on Thursday hailed what he said was a sea change in Britain's attitude towards human rights in the former Portuguese colony.

But Horta, speaking after talks with Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, said he was under no illusions that a total ban by the new Labour government was likely soon on arms sales to Indonesia, which annexed East Timor in 1975.
"We understand the dilemmas facing the British government. We don't expect them overnight to stop all arms deliveries to Indonesia," Horta told Reuters.

However, he was hopeful that Britain would block the export of certain types of weapons that he said were used by Indonesian troops in East Timor, including Land Rovers with mounted machine guns, armoured vehicles and water cannons.
Indonesia is shaping up as a litmus test of Cook's vow to put human rights at the heart of British foreign policy, and although he won no assurances Horta said he was heartened by what he heard.

He said the meeting was the first time a British foreign secretary had agreed to see independence leaders since East Timor was annexed in 1975. The international community does not recognise the annexation.
The previous Conservative British government, which was swept from power in the May 1 election after 18 years of office, regularly blocked initiatives by Portugal over East Timor, Horta said.
"That is gone, so that is an enormous change," he said. "You can say that an adversary has disappeared."
Horta said he believed Cook, by contrast, would offer more active diplomatic support for U.N.-sponsored talks between Portugal and talks on Timor, which have dragged on since 1983.
"On that front he seemed to be genuinely committed and has the ability to lead the rest of the European Union," he said.
The Foreign Office said Cook told Horta he would continue to raise Britain's concerns about human rights, as he did with Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas in Hong Kong last month.

"The Foreign Secretary reiterated his concern about the recent armed attacks, kidnappings and deaths in East Timor, all of which could only harm the prospects for political progress," the ministry said in a statement.
Horta said he hoped Britain would withdraw an invitation to the commander in chief of Indonesia's armed forces, General Feisal Tanjung, to attend a big arms show in September.
He said it would be especially inappropriate to invite Tanjung given the lead Britain took in Thursday's operation by NATO forces in Bosnia against two wanted war crimes suspects.
"Be it in Bosnia or Rwanda or Cambodia or elsewhere, the time comes when certain decisive forceful actions have to be taken for the international community to be credible," he said.
